I created https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/ to move wheel building out of this repo. Once it's all configure, this is what releasing will look like:

1. In this repo, create a new release branch and prepare it for release. Open any PRs and merge in changes.
2. Trigger the [Publish sdist and wheels](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/actions/workflows/wheels.yml) with the "chain" option. Also set `ref` to the branch name on `scikit-learn/scikit-learn`.
3. With the "chain" option, the wheels are built first and stored as artifacts. The Github UI will need a release manager to trigger the publish to `testpypi`.
    - The "chain" will publish to `testpypi` first and then `pypi` afterwards.
4. After testpypi publish succeeds, push a tag to `scikit-learn/scikit-learn` for the release.
5. In the Github UI, the release manager triggers the final publish to `pypi`.

### Plan

- [X] release development wheels from scikit-learn-release. Done since August 2026 https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/pull/5 and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34593
- [x] release 1.9.1 from scikit-learn-release https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34898
- [ ] release 1.10.0 from scikit-learn-release scheduled around November/December 2026
	- [ ] Update maintainer release instructions in scikit-learn rst files

### Other things to do at one point

- [ ] Update [README.md](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/blob/main/README.md) to do something similar to numpy
- [x] Reenable CI in `scikit-learn-release` to run all tests. I have been using `pytest --pyargs sklearn.tests.test_dummy` for a faster iteration loop. [Example](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/blob/87e247e3f11b78d3cdfb72e0dbbf191b05ca4be9/tools/test_source.sh#L17)
- [x] In [wheels.yml](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/blob/main/.github/workflows/wheels.yml), add secrets for nightly uploads for `scientific-python-nightly-wheels`

issues.title: BUG `GridSearchCV(n_jobs=8)` is 10x to 50x slower than in 1.8 on many small tasks: every task pickles the whole callback context tree
issues.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Since the callbacks API (#33322), a parallel `GridSearchCV` with many cheap fits is much slower than in 1.8. On a 2000-candidate grid on iris (10k fits of ~1 ms), `n_jobs=8` takes ~3 s on 1.8.0 but 100-150 s on 1.9.1 and 24-67 s on main. That's much slower than `n_jobs=1` (~9 s). No callback is registered.

`BaseSearchCV.fit` creates one `CallbackContext` per (candidate, split) up front and passes one to each `_fit_and_score` task. `subcontext` registers the child in the parent's `_children_map` and sets `child.parent`, so pickling one task's context pickles its parent and every sibling. The pickled task grows linearly with the number of tasks: ~50 KB per task for 500 tasks, ~420 KB per task for 5000 tasks (measured on main by pickling the `delayed` arguments `BaseSearchCV.fit` builds).

joblib pickles each batch separately, so the total pickling work is roughly (number of batches) x (number of tasks). Auto-batching hides part of it because a batch shares the pickle memo. With `pre_dispatch="all"` (batches of one task) and `refit=False`, the search takes 290 s on main, and 4.6 s with the contexts left out of the tasks.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
param_grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}  # 2000 candidates

for n_jobs in [1, 8]:
    search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(), param_grid, cv=5, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    tic = time.perf_counter()
    search.fit(X, y)
    print(f"n_jobs={n_jobs}: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.1f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Same as 1.8.0:

```
n_jobs=1: 8.7s
n_jobs=8: 3.1s
```

### Actual Results

1.9.1:

```
n_jobs=1: 10.9s
n_jobs=8: 105.9s
```

`n_jobs=8` varies a lot between runs: 100.6 s, 105.9 s and 151.1 s on 1.9.1, and 23.8 s, 31.9 s and 67.2 s on main. 1.8.0 is stable at 3.0-3.1 s. Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), same Python and joblib for all three.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.14 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:27) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
   machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
        numpy: 2.5.3
        scipy: 1.18.1
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No

issues.title: BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.
issues.author: Chaptyziok

comments.body: I've gone through the issue and the proposed fix looks clear Pipeline.fit_predict directly accesses routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]] instead of using _get_metadata_for_step like fit and fit_transform do. I'd like to work on implementing the fix along with the regression test if maintainers confirm this is the right approach.

issues.title: BUG: StandardScaler.partial_fit replaces an existing variance with NaN when a new dense batch has an all-NaN feature
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm exploring numerical reliability in scientific Python through AI-assisted investigation and testing.
This issue came from checking how StandardScaler.partial_fit handles batches with missing observations and comparing incremental results with batch fitting.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

After StandardScaler learns valid statistics for a feature, a subsequent dense batch containing only NaNs in that feature changes its var_ and scale_ to NaN, while its mean_ and sample count remain correct.

In the recorded checks, this also causes finite values in that feature to be transformed to NaN.

The StandardScaler documentation states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting. The example below supplies no new valid observations for the first feature.

Documentation:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html

Related work:
PR #16466 included preserving sparse incremental statistics when a new batch contributes zero valid observations, including all-NaN second-batch tests. This report concerns the dense-array counterpart.
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16466

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

A = np.array([[1., 10.], [3., 20.]])
B = np.array([[np.nan, 30.], [np.nan, 40.]])

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.partial_fit(A)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_, [1., 25.])

scaler.partial_fit(B)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_[0], 1.)
```

### Expected Results

The final assertion should pass. After processing B, the first feature should retain its mean of 2, variance of 1, scale of 1, and sample count of 2, because B contains no new non-missing observations for that feature.

The second feature should have a mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4.

### Actual Results

The final assertion fails because the variance of the first feature becomes NaN.

After processing B, the first feature has a mean of 2, variance of NaN, scale of NaN, and sample count of 2. The mean and sample count remain correct, but the previously valid variance and scale are lost.

The second feature has the expected mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4.

The update also emits RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in divide.

### Versions

issues.title: HistGradientBoostingClassifier: multiclass training loss diverges at default hyperparameters (LightGBM/XGBoost at equivalent settings do not)
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

On Covertype, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` with **every hyperparameter at its default** (only `max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0` set) reaches a minimum *training* log-loss of 0.418 at iteration 55, and then **rises**: 1.08 at iteration 100, 1.93 at 200. 87 of the 200 iterations increase the training loss, and leaf values reach 2.2e4. The fit is deterministic (a second fit is bit-identical) and gives identical numbers on aarch64 (AWS Graviton4) and x86. On the full dataset with `max_leaf_nodes=255` it goes 0.200 at iteration 40 → 0.817 at 100, with leaves reaching 5.7e4.

LightGBM 4.7.0 and XGBoost 3.4.2, configured through scikit-learn's own `get_equivalent_estimator` (l2 = 0; XGBoost's learning rate doubled for its 2p(1−p) hessian), decrease monotonically on the same rows, to 0.16 and 0.15.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_covtype
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss

X, y = fetch_covtype(return_X_y=True)
idx = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(y))[:20000]
X, y = X[idx, :10], y[idx]            # 10 numeric features, 7 classes

m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
for k, p in enumerate(m.staged_predict_proba(X), 1):
    if k in (25, 50, 55, 100, 200):
        print(k, round(log_loss(y, p, labels=m.classes_), 4))
```

The exact script that produced the numbers here (it also does the parameter sweep and the LightGBM/XGBoost comparison) is [hgb_repro.py](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/scientific-codes-cookbook/blob/main/measurements/scikit-learn-real/hgb-repro/hgb_repro.py), and [hgb-repro.log](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/scientific-codes-cookbook/blob/main/measurements/scikit-learn-real/hgb-repro/hgb-repro.log) is its output (scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5).

### Expected Results

Training loss that does not increase for dozens of iterations at default settings, as with LightGBM/XGBoost at equivalent settings.

### Actual Results

`25: 0.4847, 50: 0.4380, (min 0.4180 @ 55), 100: 1.0845, 200: 1.9335`

### What makes it go away (one change at a time)

- **Fixes it:** `l2_regularization` ≥ 0.01; `min_hessian_to_split` ≥ 0.01 (patched into `TreeGrower`, as it isn't an estimator parameter); `learning_rate=0.05`; a zero baseline instead of the log class priors; **`min_samples_leaf=1`**.
- **Does not fix it:** `max_leaf_nodes` 7, 15 or 255 (255 is worst); `min_samples_leaf` 5 or 100; `min_hessian_to_split=0.002`. `learning_rate=0.2` makes it worse.

At `min_samples_leaf=1`, sklearn and LightGBM agree (0.155 vs 0.152 at iteration 200). At 5 and 20, only sklearn diverges. A likely reason: LightGBM checks `min_data_in_leaf` against bin counts *estimated from hessians* (`cnt_factor = num_data / sum_hessian` in `feature_histogram.hpp`), while sklearn uses true counts. sklearn can therefore build ~20–40-row leaves whose hessian sum is barely above `min_hessian_to_split=1e-3`. In the first rising iteration (20), one such leaf has 34 rows, G = 2.0, H = 1.05e-3 and a step of −191. That is my reading of the evidence, not a verified root cause.

With the default `early_stopping='auto'`, the fit stops at `n_iter_=11` (training loss 0.64), with leaf values already at 1.9e3.

Possible remedies: a documentation note on `l2_regularization`/`min_samples_leaf` for multiclass; a small non-zero default `l2_regularization` (XGBoost defaults to `lambda=1`); or exposing `min_hessian_to_split`.

### Versions

scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, Python 3.14 (conda-forge), on linux-aarch64 and linux-64. Results are identical on both.
issues.author: scttfrdmn

comments.body:
I tested an alternative to the listed remedies: **conditionally safeguard the fitted leaf values while retaining the existing defaults and split rules**. After fitting all class trees for a round, I evaluated the multinomial training loss directly from the raw logits. If it has not  increased, I retain the proposed updates. Otherwise, I repair that round by clipping its leaf values. The repair keeps the fitted partitions  and does not grow replacement trees.

The clipping has a sufficient descent argument. For a class-specific leaf, let $P$ be its weighted predicted class mass and $N$ its weighted  observed class count. For simultaneously added class-tree updates $v$, the change in summed weighted loss satisfies

$$
\Delta L\leq\sum_{\text{class-specific leaves}}
\left[P(e^v-1)-Nv\right].
$$

For $P,N>0$, clipping each update to the interval between zero and $\log(N/P)$ makes every term nonpositive. Zero-mass cases require separate handling. This gives a sufficient descent condition for nonnegative weights in exact arithmetic.

On the original Covertype reproducer:

| After 200 rounds | Original | Safeguarded |
|---|---:|---:|
| `log_loss` from probabilities | 1.93347 | 0.15644 |
| Logit-space loss without probability clipping | 196.42444 | 0.15644 |
| Largest absolute leaf value | 21,480 | 16.20 |

issues.title: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

comments.body:
It seems the cause isn't in scikit-learn or dpnp. Two things combine:

1. `array_api_strict.from_dlpack(x, device=...)` checks `device` but doesn't pass it on to `np.from_dlpack` ([source](https://github.com/data-apis/array-api-strict/blob/ef5d7dbb8d5585438c27a0ba167bc7e32361c104/array_api_strict/_creation_functions.py#L249-L256)). Without a `device`, NumPy calls `x.__dlpack__(dl_device=None)`, so dpnp exports the data on its SYCL device (`kDLOneAPI`), as the protocol requires. When the consumer asks for `dl_device=(kDLCPU, 0)`, dpnp copies to host, e.g. `np.from_dlpack(dpnp.arange(3), device="cpu")` works.
2. NumPy can't import a non-CPU capsule, so raising is correct. But NumPy <= 2.4 raises `RuntimeError` instead of `BufferError`. `move_to` doesn't catch `RuntimeError`, so the `_convert_to_numpy` fallback is skipped. NumPy 2.5.0 raises `BufferError` instead (numpy/numpy#31000).

CPU torch tensors don't hit this because they already export as `kDLCPU`.

**Minimal reproducer without scikit-learn**

```python
import dpnp
import array_api_strict as xp

y = dpnp.arange(3)
xp.from_dlpack(y, device=xp.Device("CPU_DEVICE"))
# numpy <= 2.4: RuntimeError: Unsupported device in DLTensor.
# numpy >= 2.5: BufferError: Unsupported device in DLTensor.
```

NumPy alone shows the same thing: `np.from_dlpack(y)` fails, while `np.from_dlpack(y, device="cpu")` works.

**Suggestions**

- NumPy >= 2.5 fixes the reported case.
- scikit-learn could also catch `RuntimeError` until the minimum NumPy is >= 2.5, like the existing `ValueError` TODO.
- Separately, array-api-strict could pass an explicit `device` to NumPy as `np.from_dlpack(x, device="cpu", copy=copy)`, which is valid since all its devices are host-backed. Then the DLPack path itself would work, with no fallback needed. I tried this as a local patch on NumPy 2.4.6: `move_to` works, and `copy=False` still raises `BufferError` as expected.

`BaseRandomProjection.fit` ends with `self._n_features_out = self.n_components`. With the default `n_components="auto"` this stores the string `"auto"` instead of the inferred `n_components_`. import numpy as np

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`numpy.dtypes.StringDType` (and other new-style DType classes) crash `xp.isdtype()` across many sklearn utilities.

`numpy`'s (and array-api-compat's) `isdtype()` raises `TypeError` instead of returning `False` for numpy's new-style DType classes. sklearn calls `xp.isdtype(...)` in many places expecting `False` for unrecognized dtypes, not a crash.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
np.isdtype(np.dtypes.StringDType(), "numeric")
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

```python
from sklearn.utils.multiclass import type_of_target
type_of_target(np.array(["a", "b", "a"], dtype=np.dtypes.StringDType()))
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

Confirmed crash sites (14), all via `xp.isdtype()` except `unique_labels`:

| Function | File |
|---|---|
| `check_array` (any `dtype=`, incl. `None`) | `utils/validation.py` |
| `type_of_target` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_is_integral_float` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_assert_all_finite` | `utils/validation.py` |
| `_randomized_range_finder` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_safe_accumulator_op` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_find_matching_floating_dtype` | `utils/_array_api.py` |

Related: #34383 (motivation — proposes `StringDType` internally in encoders), #9777 (same failure pattern, closed).

issues.title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

### Actual Results

```
1.9.1
importances_mean (max_samples=0.5): [ 1.7655429  -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):
[[-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
 [-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]]
importances_mean (max_samples=1.0): [1.79471992 0.         0.        ]
baseline (all rows) r2: 0.9095261981105188
max_samples=0.2: importances_mean = [ 1.76648851 -0.02631336 -0.02631336]  importances_std = [0.30605997 0.         0.        ]
max_samples=0.1: importances_mean = [1.66914758 0.00620688 0.00620688]  importances_std = [0.73546823 0.         0.        ]
```

### Versions


comments.body: I reproduced this (unused features get -0.0104 at max_samples=0.5, exactly 0 at 1.0) and confirmed the root cause: the baseline is scored on all rows while permuted scores use a single shared subsample, so the full-vs-subsample gap leaks into every importance. I have a fix ready (score the baseline on the same up-front subsample; all 36 existing permutation-importance tests still pass, plus a new regression test). comments.body:
Proposal for discussion (per the contributing guide), before any implementation PR:

**Problem.** With `max_samples < n_samples`, the baseline is scored on all rows while each permuted score uses one shared row subsample (drawn once per column from the same seed, hence std of exactly 0). The full-vs-subsample gap leaks into every importance, so features the model never reads get non-zero values (e.g. -0.0104 at max_samples=0.5, exactly 0 at 1.0).

**Proposed fix.** Draw the shared subsample once up front (same seed workers use, so rows are unchanged) and score the baseline on it; hand workers the already-subsampled data so permutations proceed as before. Importances then measure only the permutation effect: unused features become exactly 0, full-sample behavior is untouched.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) Fresh subsample per repeat + per-repeat baseline: matches the "in each repeat" docstring more literally but changes sampling behavior and more test expectations. (b) Leave as-is and document the bias: keeps a silently misleading default.

Happy to implement the proposed fix (plus a regression test) if maintainers agree with this direction.

issues.title: BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

Hello, I am using sklearn for the forecasting project and in the meantime found some issues I reported here. 

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

issues.title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
issues.body:
> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. I'm about to open a PR with a proposed fixed: detecting high mean/variance ratio and explicitly recentering if needed.

comments.body:
> How do other libraries compare here (R glm, R glmnet, statsmodels, H2O, skglm, celer)?

That's a very good question!

Claude ran the same kind of sweep on all of them: one dataset (n=5000, 5 standard-normal features, a logistic target and a Poisson target), adding an offset to every feature from 1 to 1e6. For each library, it compared `coef` to that same library's fit at offset 0. it also read the docs and the sources to check whether they center.

Versions: R 4.5.3, glmnet 5.0, statsmodels 0.15.0, H2O 3.46.0.12, skglm 0.5, celer 0.7.4, and sklearn 1.9.1 as the baseline.

### Summary

| Library | Centers X? | Solver | Behavior with a large offset |
|---|---|---|-----------------------------------------|
| **R `glm`** | No | IRLS; each step is a Householder QR of the weighted design, and X'WX is never formed | Robust: rel. err. ~1e-11 at offset 1e6 |
| **R `glmnet`** | **Yes**, whenever `intercept=TRUE`, even with `standardize=FALSE`. For sparse X the centering is done implicitly inside the CD updates. | Coordinate descent on the centered data | Robust: ~1e-11 at 1e6 |
| **statsmodels `GLM`** (IRLS, the default) | No | IRLS with `lstsq` (SVD) on the weighted design | Robust: ~1e-11 at 1e6 |
| statsmodels `GLM(method="lbfgs")` | No | L-BFGS, but warm-started with 3 IRLS iterations (`max_start_irls=3`) | Stays at the tolerance level (~4e-4) across the whole range, thanks to the IRLS warm start |
| statsmodels `Logit` / `Poisson` (newton, the default) | No | Newton with an explicit Hessian and `np.linalg.solve` | Breaks at ~1e4 (Poisson) / ~3e4 (Logit), with a `ConvergenceWarning` |
| statsmodels `Logit(method="bfgs")` | No | BFGS | Breaks at ~100-300, with a `ConvergenceWarning` |
| **H2O GLM**, `standardize=True` (the default) | **Yes** | IRLSM (Cholesky of the Gram matrix) or L-BFGS | Robust for both solvers |
| H2O GLM, `standardize=False` | No | IRLSM | Degrades gradually, roughly like offset² · eps: 2e-3 at 5.6e5 |
| H2O GLM, `standardize=False` | No | L-BFGS | **Garbage from offset ~30** (binomial) / ~18 (Poisson). Only one warning was raised over the whole sweep ("Reached maximum number of iterations 20!") |
| **skglm** (sparse logistic regression, `Lasso`, Poisson with ProxNewton) | No; the intercept is one more coordinate with its own 1-D update | CD / prox-Newton | `coef` stays at the tolerance level, but **fit time grows ~offset²**. |
| **celer** `Lasso` | Yes, because it subclasses sklearn's `Lasso` and reuses `_preprocess_data` | CD with working sets | Identical to sklearn's `Lasso` |
| celer `LogisticRegression` | Not applicable | | `fit_intercept=True` raises `NotImplementedError`, so the problem can't occur |

Documentation: **no library mentions a numerical need to center**.
- glmnet documents `standardize` but not the centering that happens regardless of it.
- H2O "highly recommends" `standardize=True`, but the reason it gives is penalty scale, not conditioning.
- statsmodels only prints the generic "condition number is large" note, and only in the OLS summary.
- R `glm`, skglm and celer say nothing about it.

### Takeaways

1 - The libraries that are robust get there in one of two ways:
  - they center X internally (glmnet always, H2O by default, celer through sklearn);
  - or they use IRLS with an orthogonal factorization of the weighted design (R `glm`, statsmodels `GLM`), which never forms X'WX.

2 - Other approaches degrade like sklearn does:
  - statsmodels Logit/Poisson and bfgs, H2O `standardize=False` + L-BFGS, and skglm, where the damage shows up as run time rather than accuracy.
  - statsmodels at least raises a `ConvergenceWarning`. H2O L-BFGS and skglm are essentially silent.

3 - In float64, sklearn's `lbfgs` (broken from offset ~100-200) is in the same range as the worst of these (statsmodels bfgs, H2O L-BFGS without standardization). It's much worse than R `glm`, glmnet, statsmodels' default `GLM`, or H2O's default.

comments.body:
This still reproduces on 1.9.1 with scipy 1.17.1 (the scipy message is now ABNORMAL:  rather than ABNORMAL_TERMINATION_IN_LNSRCH, but the code path is still the same). Three observations that may be usful before #34891 is merged:

### 1. It is not limited to data whose optimal scale is zero

In the original report all three y are equal, so the minimiser sits on the lower bound of the feasible set. That is a natural suspect, but the same failure appears on ordinary data whose optimal scale is far from the bound. The only thing that has to change is the magnitude of X:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import optimize
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model._huber import _huber_loss_and_gradient

# Case 1 -- three samples, x of the order of 100.
X1 = np.array([15.0, 75.0, 150.0]).reshape(-1, 1)
y1 = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])

# Case 2 -- nine samples, three outliers, optimal scale is about 130.
X2 = np.array([980.191, 1609.435, 4263.953, 4908.433, 5485.004,
               6194.265, 6995.905, 7233.989, 7584.523]).reshape(-1, 1)
y2 = np.array([-78.963, 227.826, -502.425, -109.711, -85.640,
               194.003, -29.175, -24.662, 364.737])

for name, X, y, factor in [("case 1", X1, y1, 10.0), ("case 2", X2, y2, 100.0)]:
    try:
        HuberRegressor().fit(X, y)
        print(name, "raw X: no error")
    except ValueError as exc:
        print(name, "raw X:", exc)
    m = HuberRegressor().fit(X / factor, y)
    print(name, "X / %g: coef_=%.8g intercept_=%.8g scale_=%.8g n_iter_=%d"
          % (factor, m.coef_[0] / factor, m.intercept_, m.scale_, m.n_iter_))

# What L-BFGS-B returns for case 2, i.e. what fit() would expose if the
# ValueError were replaced by a ConvergenceWarning.
p = np.zeros(3)
p[-1] = 1.0
bounds = np.tile([-np.inf, np.inf], (3, 1))
bounds[-1][0] = np.finfo(np.float64).eps * 10
res = optimize.minimize(
    _huber_loss_and_gradient, p, method="L-BFGS-B", jac=True,
    args=(X2, y2, 1.35, 1e-4, np.ones(len(y2))),
    options={"maxiter": 100, "gtol": 1e-5}, bounds=bounds,
)
print("case 2 last iterate: status=%d nit=%d coef=%.8g intercept=%.8g scale=%.8g"
      % (res.status, res.nit, res.x[0], res.x[1], res.x[2]))
```

Output:

```
case 1 raw X: HuberRegressor convergence failed: l-BFGS-b solver terminated with ABNORMAL: 
case 1 X / 10: coef_=0.01481529 intercept_=0.77775631 scale_=9.4400188e-05 n_iter_=41
case 2 raw X: HuberRegressor convergence failed: l-BFGS-b solver terminated with ABNORMAL: 
case 2 X / 100: coef_=0.01445875 intercept_=-69.794599 scale_=129.73122 n_iter_=27
case 2 last iterate: status=2 nit=3 coef=-0.0039630149 intercept=-2.3917343e-05 scale=1.0000641
```

In case 2 the optimal scale is about 130, nowhere near the bound, and the fit after dividing X by 100 converges in 27 iterations. So the trigger is not the degeneracy of the data but the starting point. fit always starts L-BFGS-B at `coef=0, intercept=0, sigma=1`, independently of the data. When y is of the order of a hundred, every residual at that point is an outlier, and the gradient with respect to the coefficients is of the order of `2 * epsilon * sum(|X|)` — about 1.2e5 for case 2. The first line search is then asked to move a long way along a very steep direction, and it gives up.

I scanned 17568 random single-feature problems (n from 3 to 60, X spanning from 1e-2 to 1e4, y spanning from 1e-2 to 1e3, with and without ties and outliers): 12 of them raise this ValueError, roughly one in 1500. All 12 fit without any warning once X is divided by a constant, and all 12 fit when X is standardised. In other words the error is raised on problems that are well posed; only the conditioning of the starting point is bad.

### 2. What fitting would return once the raise is removed?

#34891 deletes the raise so that `_check_optimize_result` emits a ConvergenceWarning and fit keeps the last iterate. It may be worth checking what that iterate is on these inputs. For case 2 above L-BFGS-B stops after 3 iterations at `coef=-0.0039630149, intercept=-2.3917343e-05, scale=1.0000641`, against `coef=0.014458750, intercept=-69.794599, scale=129.73122` for the same problem solved after rescaling: the slope has the wrong sign, the intercept is essentially zero, and `scale_` is still the initial value. On other instances in the scan the line search fails at nit=0, in which case `coef_`, `intercept_` and `scale_` are exactly the initial 0/0/1 — a warning and an unfitted model.

The consistency argument for warning rather than raising is a good one, and I am not arguing against the change. But a ConvergenceWarning from LogisticRegression usually means "stopped early, the iterate is usable", while here it can mean "never moved". If the change goes in, it may be worth treating nit=0 separately, or saying in the warning that the returned coefficients may still be the initial ones.

I also tried starting the solver from `coef=0, intercept=median(y), sigma=1.4826 * MAD(y)`. On 5265 problems from the same scan it removes all four line-search failures, and among the problems where both starting points converge it more often ends lower than higher (better by more than 1e-3 relative on 25% of them, worse on 6%). But the rest is bad: on 2.6% it ends more than 1% above the other starting point, and in the worst case by two orders of magnitude. So it is not a drop-in replacement, and changing the initialisation would need its own investigation rather than being folded into this fix.

### 3. The same conditioning problem can produce a wrong fit with no error at all

The failure does not always raise. On a feature with a large offset the solver can stop at a point that is nowhere near the minimum while reporting success, so fit returns a model that looks fitted and is not. The data below is an exact line with no noise and no outliers, and the feature is an ordinary one: a millisecond timestamp.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor, LinearRegression

t = np.linspace(1.7e12, 1.7e12 + 20_000.0, 24).reshape(-1, 1)
y = 0.002 * (t.ravel() - t[0, 0]) + 5.0      # exact line, no noise, no outliers

huber = HuberRegressor().fit(t, y)
print("huber  coef:", huber.coef_[0], "n_iter:", huber.n_iter_, "R2:", huber.score(t, y))
print("linear coef:", LinearRegression().fit(t, y).coef_[0])

mu = t.mean()
print("huber on centred feature coef:", HuberRegressor().fit(t - mu, y).coef_[0])
```

Output:

```
huber  coef: 1.4705882295609986e-11 n_iter: 5 R2: 1.4705882178667196e-08
linear coef: 0.002
huber on centred feature coef: 0.0019999999999763493
```

No warning is emitted, `n_iter_` is 5 and the object exposes a coefficient that is eight orders of magnitude away from the least-squares solution, on data where the Huber optimum and the least-squares solution coincide. Sweeping the magnitude of an exact line `y = -1e-6 * x + 50` over 20 points gives, with no warning at any row:

```
1e3  coef=-1e-06         rel.err=2.72e-07
1e4  coef=-1e-06         rel.err=3.4e-06
1e5  coef=-1e-06         rel.err=7.61e-12
1e6  coef= 2.71828e-05   rel.err=28.2
1e7  coef= 1.82029e-06   rel.err=2.82
1e8  coef=-3.13577e-07   rel.err=0.686
1e9  ValueError: ... terminated with ABNORMAL:
1e10 coef=-9.93136e-07   rel.err=0.00686
1e11 ValueError: ... terminated with ABNORMAL:
1e12 ValueError: ... terminated with ABNORMAL:
```

At 1e6 and 1e7 the sign of the coefficient is wrong. `tol` between 1e-5 and 1e-15 and `max_iter` between 100 and 10000 change nothing: the solver stops after 5 iterations in every combination.

This matters for #34891 specifically. Turning the ValueError into a ConvergenceWarning addresses the rows that raise, but the rows above that return silently are the same underlying problem and would still be silent afterwards.

---

Btw, the class docstring says "Note that this does not take into account the fact that the different features of X may be of different scales", and the user guide says HuberRegressor "is scaling invariant". Both statements are about epsilon and about features relative to each other. Neither tells the reader that the absolute magnitude of a single feature can decide whether fit raises. A sentence recommending that X be standardised, next to the note that is already there, would be useful independently of what happens to the solver.
